meta.title: The rocket for NASA's next moon landing is ahead of schedule. The spacesuit is not.
meta.subtitle: Technicians began bolting shuttle-flown engines into the Artemis 3 rocket this week, comfortably on pace. The suit astronauts would need to actually walk on the moon has a schedule of its own, and NASA's inspector general does not believe it.
meta.push_title: The Artemis rocket is on schedule. The suit may not be.
meta.push_body: NASA's own inspector general says the moon suit contract is tracking toward 2031, three years after the 2028 landing target.

body:
Inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center on August 24, technicians began lowering the first of four RS-25 engines into the core stage of the rocket that will fly the Artemis 3 crew. All four have flown before. Engine 2048 previously powered space shuttle missions including STS-95 in 1998, which carried Senator John Glenn, and STS-129 in 2009, whose pilot was Randy Bresnik. Bresnik is training to command Artemis 3.

The engines are one of several pieces of hardware converging on schedule. None of it will touch the moon. NASA restructured Artemis 3 in February, removing the landing and turning the mission into a rendezvous and docking test in Earth orbit between Orion and commercial landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin. The actual landing, the first since 1972, moved to Artemis 4, which NASA still targets for early 2028.

What Artemis 4 needs that Artemis 3 does not is a spacesuit rated to keep a human alive on the lunar surface. In April, NASA's Office of Inspector General (OIG) published an audit concluding the agency is unlikely to have one in time.

---

**Get the next briefing in your inbox. [Subscribe free →](https://artemis-briefing.kit.com)**

---

## Heritage engines, new mission

Each RS-25 weighs about 7,700 pounds (3,490 kilograms) and produces close to 500,000 pounds of thrust (2,224 kilonewtons), burning for more than eight minutes and consuming roughly 1,500 gallons (5,680 liters) of propellant every second. All four assigned to Artemis 3, engines 2048, 2052, 2054 and 2057, are shuttle veterans rather than new builds, which is why NASA can fly them again without waiting years for fresh engines off a production line.

The rest of the vehicle is converging at a similar pace. Solid rocket booster segments are more than halfway stacked on the mobile launcher. Orion's crew and service modules, joined on July 30, are being outfitted in parallel. Bresnik, fellow NASA astronauts Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio, and European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Luca Parmitano have trained since their June 9 crew assignment, including spacesuit egress drills in the Neutral Buoyancy Lab and integrated simulations with the flight control team. Administrator Jared Isaacman said in August he was "extremely confident" the mission would fly next year, and the hardware in the Vehicle Assembly Building backs him up.

## One bidder left

The spacesuit program started from a different position. In May 2022, NASA awarded services contracts worth a combined $3.1 billion to two companies, Axiom Space and Collins Aerospace, under the Exploration Extravehicular Activity Services (xEVAS) program. Axiom received a $228 million order that September to build a lunar surface suit, the Axiom Extravehicular Mobility Unit (AxEMU), unveiled in its flight design with fashion house Prada in October 2024. Collins received $97 million in December 2022 to build a separate suit for spacewalks outside the International Space Station (ISS).

Collins never got there. NASA and the company agreed in 2024 to drop its task orders, citing an inability to meet the ISS demonstration schedule. That left Axiom as the sole remaining supplier under a contract built around two competitors, and the sole path to a suit for Artemis 4.

## The 8.7-year average

The OIG's report, published April 20 and numbered IG-26-006, does not claim to know when AxEMU will be ready. It instead measured how long comparable NASA programs have actually taken, from contract award to first flight, across six analogous efforts including Orion, Commercial Crew and the Space Launch System (SLS) itself. The average came to 8.7 years. Applied to the xEVAS award date of May 2022, that points to a demonstration around mid-2031, three years after the Artemis 4 landing target. Drop the Commercial Cargo program from the sample, on the argument that cargo delivery is not a fair comparison to a crewed suit, and the average rises to 10.2 years, pushing the projection to mid-2032.

"If Axiom experiences design and testing delays in line with the historical average for recent space flight programs," the report states, "the Artemis and ISS demonstrations may not occur until 2031." The audit's two recommendations were narrower than that headline number: seek industry input to preserve competition for future spacesuit contracts, and develop interoperability standards between Artemis landers and whatever suit ultimately flies. Neither recommendation carried a dollar figure or a demand to change the current schedule.

## 950 hours of testing

Axiom's own account, given days before the audit's release, was considerably more confident. The company said it had nearly finished AxEMU's critical design review and was on track for a demonstration in 2027, either on the ISS or during Artemis 3, and cited more than 950 hours of crewed pressurized testing completed to date. "It's about as close as we can get to actual spaceflight on the ground," Russell Ralston, Axiom's senior vice president for extravehicular activity, said of the testing. Axiom chief executive Jonathan Cirtain put it more directly: "The agency has made it clear we're going to fly a suit next year." Isaacman, for his part, has described the value of an early flight test in modest terms: "Even just getting an astronaut in a suit in microgravity, we can learn a lot."

It is worth being precise about what a 2027 demonstration would actually prove. Artemis 3 no longer lands, so a suit worn on that mission would be tested in microgravity or during a docked spacewalk, not on the surface. The lunar-specific problems the OIG flagged, including the extreme cold of the south pole's permanently shadowed regions and eight-hour surface excursions, would still be unproven going into Artemis 4. A successful 2027 test would be real progress. It would not close the gap between a demonstration and a certified, produced-in-quantity suit ready for a landing the following year, and the OIG's historical comparison is specifically about programs that struggled in that stretch.

## The next checkpoints

Two schedules are now running in parallel toward the same mission. Artemis 3 is due to fly its Earth-orbit rendezvous late next year, with SLS, Orion, Blue Origin's Blue Moon and SpaceX's Starship all expected to participate in some combination of dockings. Somewhere in that same window, Axiom intends to put AxEMU through its first crewed flight test. Artemis 4, carrying the landing itself, remains targeted for early 2028, a date NASA says has not moved since mid-2025. Whether it holds depends less on any of the hardware currently going into the Vehicle Assembly Building than on whether a suit still in design review can beat a track record that says it usually takes years longer than planned.

The engines going into the Artemis 3 core stage this week are a known process. NASA has flown RS-25s for decades, on the shuttle and now on SLS, and installing four more into a rocket is not the part of this program that keeps slipping. The spacesuit is a new design, built by a company that was supposed to have a competitor and no longer does, aimed at a deadline that assumes nothing goes wrong from here. Nothing about bolting in an engine changes that.
